title: Bar Harbor Airlines 1808
summary: Bar Harbor Airlines Flight 1808, a Beechcraft Model 99, departed Logan International Airport in Boston for Bangor, Maine, with planned stops in Augusta and Waterville, including an unscheduled flag stop in Auburn/Lewiston. At 22:00 EDT, weather at Auburn consisted of a 300-foot obscured indefinite ceiling, 1-mile visibility, and light drizzle. A Portland controller advised the flight it was drifting east of the ILS approach course and instructed a heading of 340 degrees. The aircraft flew through the approach course, requiring a 60-degree right turn less than 1 nautical mile from the outer marker. The aircraft did not begin descent until after passing Lewiston, already above the glide slope, causing the crew to rush the descent and approach with a steep descent profile. The aircraft crashed into trees 4,007 feet from the runway end and 440 feet to the right of centerline. All eight people on board were killed.
probable_cause: The captain's continuation of an unstabilized approach which resulted in a descent below glideslope. Contributing to the unstabilized approach was the radar controller's issuance and the captain's acceptance of a nonstandard air traffic control radar vector resulting in an excessive intercept with the localizer (p. 59)

recommendations.text: Establish for aircraft used in commercial operation the maximum cockpit noise levels which will permit adequate direct voice communication between flight crewmembers under all operating conditions.

Require the installation and use of crew interphone systems in the cockpits of those aircraft in which noise levels reach or exceed the maximum level established for adequate direct voice communication between flight crewmembers under all operating conditions.

Require that all multiengine, turbine-powered, fixed-wing aircraft certificated to carry six or more passengers manufactured on or after a specified date be prewired to accept a cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.

Require that general aviation cockpit voice recorders and flight data recorders be installed when commercially available as standard equipment in all multiengine, turbine-powered fixed-wing aircraft and rotorcraft certificated to carry six or more passengers.

Require that general aviation cockpit voice recorders be installed as soon as commercially available in all multiengine, turbine-powered aircraft certificated to carry six or more passengers and required to have two pilots.
